problems.title: Kinds of dependence
hints: Which order must be kept, and why?
problems.solution: RAW is real data flow; WAR and WAW exist only because a name is reused, and renaming removes them.

problems.title: Moving independent work
problems.statement: One warp: ld x; y = fma(x); i0 … i5 = six independent FMAs.
hints: As written, the independent FMAs wait behind the dependent one.
problems.solution: (a) 410: y waits until 400, and the six FMAs queue behind it. (b) 404: the FMAs issue during the load. The load's latency dominates either way, but the scheduler removed everything after it.

problems.title: Hoisting loads
problems.statement: One warp: ld a; use a; ld b; use b, versus ld a; ld b; use a; use b.
hints: Two loads in flight at once.
problems.solution: 805 versus 405: hoisting both loads overlaps their latencies, nearly halving the time. This is what unrolling plus scheduling buys a single warp.

problems.title: Critical-path priorities
problems.statement: Block: l = ld (400); m = mul(l); n = add(m); p = fma (independent); q = fma(p). Priority = longest latency path to the end.
problems.solution: (a) 408, (b) 8. The load issues first; p and q fill the wait. Makespan 408: the critical path plus one issue cycle for l.

problems.title: Warps or ILP
problems.statement: Hide a 400-cycle load per 100 cycles of independent work per iteration.

parts.prompt: Warps needed with one load per warp in flight?
With 4 independent loads per warp (unrolled), warps needed?

hints: (C + L)/C, then divide by the loads in flight.
problems.solution: (a) $(100 + 400)/100 = 5$. (b) $5/4 = 1.25$, so 2 warps. Same idle slots, filled by either mechanism.

problems.title: Renaming costs registers
problems.statement: A loop body reuses one temporary t for 4 loads in sequence (load t, use t, load t, use t, …).

parts.prompt: Can the 4 loads be hoisted together as written?
options: No: the reuse of t creates anti/output dependences

parts.prompt: Registers for the temporaries after renaming to t0–t3?

hints: Each in-flight load needs its own destination.
problems.solution: The shared name serialises the loads. Renaming to 4 registers lets all 4 be in flight: ILP paid for in registers.

problems.title: Software pipelining
problems.statement: A loop: each iteration loads (400 cycles latency) then computes for 50 cycles on the loaded data. 100 iterations, one warp.

parts.prompt: Loads that must be in flight to keep compute busy?

hints: Iteration k's compute overlaps loads for k+1 … k+d.
problems.solution: (a) 45,000. (b) ⌈400/50⌉ + 1 = 9 loads in flight. (c) About 400 + 5,000 = 5,400: 8.3× faster. The registers or shared memory for 9 stages are the price.

problems.title: Memory dependences
problems.statement: A store to out[i] is followed by a load from in[j].

parts.prompt: May the compiler move the load above the store?
options: Only if it can prove in and out don't overlap (e.g. __restrict__)

problems.solution: Without proof the pointers differ, the load might read what the store wrote. __restrict__ gives the proof, unlocking reordering and caching (Part 2's read-only path).

problems.title: Accumulator chains
problems.statement: A single warp sums with FADD (latency 4) into one accumulator.

parts.prompt: Independent accumulators needed to issue an add every cycle?
Speedup from 1 to 4 accumulators for a long sum?

problems.solution: 4 chains keep the pipeline full: ~4× faster. The compiler can't do this for floats without fast-math (it changes rounding), so you write it.

problems.title: Order matters at low occupancy
problems.statement: A register-tiled GEMM runs 4 warps per SM (1 per scheduler).

parts.prompt: Who hides shared-memory latency within a warp?
options: the instruction order chosen by ptxas, putting independent FMAs between loads and uses

problems.solution: With one warp per scheduler, nothing else can fill a gap: the schedule must, by issuing next step's loads early (or interleaving FMAs between LDS and first use). Lab 6's ILP exercise measures this.
